summary: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .

title: Rescaling OLS-Merged Adapters To Improve Personalized Image Generation
summary: Merging multiple adapters into a single image generation model reduces deployment costs while preserving diverse task capabilities or personalization modes. State-of-the-art methods such as RegMean, Mix-of-Show, and Subspace Routing fit the outputs of the merged model to those of the individual adapters using ordinary least squares (OLS). We show that this reconstruction objective systematically shrinks task-specific signals whenever the activation distributions of different tasks overlap, producing a merged adapter that is too weak for downstream use. We derive a decomposition that quantifies this shrinkage and propose rescaling the merged update to restore signal strength. On multi-subject personalization with up to 30 merged adapters, rescaling substantially improves subject fidelity over unscaled baselines. Our approach also improves results on style transfer, concept erasure, image classification, and LLM-based text classification.

title: MI-Hyper: Generating Multiple Instance Models for Weight Space Transfer Learning in Histopathology via Mixed Tasks Pretrained HyperNetwork
summary: Zero-shot whole-slide image (WSI) prediction aims to generalize to new pathology tasks without parameter updates at deployment. MI-Zero makes these predictions by pooling patch-text similarities. Conditional weight generation, combined with supervision from diverse pathology tasks, offers an alternative: learning to construct predictive rules from task descriptions. We introduce MI-Hyper, a hypernetwork pretrained across mixed tasks to generate the aggregation and classification weights of multiple instance learning (MIL) models. We first train the generator and a shared MIL basis jointly using source labels. We then freeze the basis and refine the generator. The generated task weights are reused across cases. Across 308 tasks from 52 pathology datasets, MI-Hyper improves mean AUC, balanced accuracy and macro-F1 over MI-Zero by 1.85, 1.17 and 0.57 percentage points, respectively. On some molecular prediction tasks, both AUC and balanced accuracy improve by more than 20 points. These results support task-conditioned weight generation as a promising approach to weight-space transfer for long-sequence modeling.

title: Smoothing Bias and Direction Recovery at Boundary Minima of the Nuclear Norm along Matrix Lines
summary: We study optimal matrix directions associated with minimizing $\|G+λΘ\|_*$, the nuclear norm along a fixed affine line of real matrices with scalar multiplier $λ$. At a rank-deficient minimum, the compact polar factor can violate the tangency constraint even at the minimizing multiplier. Spectral smoothing gives a continuous scalar equation for tangency. We quantify its bias at a unique boundary minimum, where exactly one one-sided derivative vanishes. An orthogonal block decomposition shows that pseudo-Huber smoothing with scale $δ$ shifts the multiplier by exact order $δ^{2/3}$ as $δ\to0$. The Frobenius error relative to the minimum-Frobenius-norm optimal direction has exact order $δ^{1/3}$ when some singular values vanish at exactly second order in the multiplier displacement, and $δ^{2/3}$ otherwise. A sharp rank bound rules out the slower rate when $Θ$ has rank at most two. Huber smoothing gives an error of exact order $δ$ for the same limiting direction. Convergent expansions in powers of $δ^{1/3}$ also yield a three-scale extrapolation with $O(δ)$ error after restoring feasibility.

title: Hierarchical Diffusion Transformer for End-to-End Image Generation
summary: Pixel-space diffusion learns visual representations and image generation jointly in a single end-to-end training stage, without a separately pretrained visual encoder. However, plain pixel-space Transformers still trail leading two-stage latent diffusion models in generation quality and training efficiency. We hypothesize that part of this gap arises from retaining one token per patch throughout the backbone, which does not explicitly encourage a visual hierarchy that summarizes related content at progressively coarser levels. To address this, we introduce Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers (HiT), which progressively group related tokens and represent each group with a single token. The main Transformer bottleneck processes these compact group tokens, and ungrouping restores features to their original image positions. A compression budget regulates the average compression ratio across the batch, allowing group memberships and counts to vary across images and diffusion timesteps during both training and generation. The model exhibits emergent semantic structure, learning to group coherent objects and object parts without segmentation labels. In text-to-image generation, HiT further learns to group caption words with image patches depicting the same concepts, without region annotations. HiT achieves 1.48 FID on ImageNet $256\times256$ and reaches comparable generation quality to JiT using approximately 40\% of its cumulative training FLOPs. For text-to-image generation, HiT exceeds UniLiP's average score across five benchmarks with roughly $6\times$ fewer denoiser parameters and $3\times$ fewer forward FLOPs. These results suggest that learning a visual hierarchy within the generator breaks down the barrier to stronger image generation without external visual pretraining.

title: A Predictive Nuclear Effective Field Theory from Wilsonian Renormalization Group Principles I: Medium-mass nuclei and nuclear matter
summary: The predictive power of nuclear effective field theory (EFT) from few- to many-body systems is substantially restricted by regulator dependence. Wilsonian momentum-shell renormalization group (RG) offers a natural framework for cutoff-independent predictions, but its many-body implementation requires regulating single-particle momentum modes, which breaks Galilean invariance. RG scaling analysis shows that this symmetry breaking is encoded in irrelevant operators whose effects can be included explicitly or absorbed into higher-body interactions. Guided by Wilsonian RG, we construct a regularization scheme for chiral EFT contact interactions and predict binding energies of nuclei up to $^{40}$Ca using interactions calibrated only to $A\leq3$ systems. The predicted energies vary at the percent level and agree with experiment for $300\leqΛ\leq450$~MeV. The same scheme reduces the overbinding of symmetric nuclear matter obtained with conventional relative-momentum regulators. Our results suggest that some model dependence observed in nonrelativistic many-body calculations originates from treating EFT vertices as static, Galilean-invariant potentials rather than as field operators regulated consistently across particle-number sectors.

title: ResoLUT: Distilling Residual Networks into Lookup-Table Networks
summary: Logic networks built from Boolean gates or lookup tables (LUTs) promise efficient hardware inference, but training them at depth and learning their connectivity remain difficult. We do not train logic as logic. Instead, ResoLUT distills a trained residual network (ResNet) layer by layer into LUT trees, preserving its multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm while extracting connectivity from the teacher rather than learning it. To our knowledge, ResoLUT is the first convolutional logic network in computer vision to retain a ResNet-style multi-bit residual stream. Hard LUT decisions are used throughout training and inference, avoiding a discretization gap in the logic. ResoLUT-20 reaches 95.66% on CIFAR-10 with twice the trees, and ResoLUT-56 reaches 78.87% on CIFAR-100 and 53.69% on ImageNet at 64px, the best results of logic and lookup-table networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, showing that LUT networks can scale in depth. We explore and quantify the role of the residuals and the tree budget and shape. The most optimized model, a ResoLUT-8 with one eighth of the trees and further optimizations, fits on an FPGA and reaches 90.04% at 189k images per second, the highest throughput among the compared models above 85% on CIFAR-10.

title: A high-dimensional spatial-physical coupling operator for generalizable super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulent flows
summary: Accurate representation of turbulent flows requires simultaneously capturing multi-scale spatial structures and the complex, nonlinear coupling between distinct physical quantities (\textit{e.g.}, velocity components and density). In practice, however, turbulent data are often constrained by low spatial resolution due to hardware limitations and computational costs. While current data-driven super-resolution methods have shown promise by learning mappings via convolutional neural networks (CNNs), they typically treat physical variables as independent channels. This simplified approach neglects intrinsic cross-variable correlations, causing models to struggle with high-fidelity reconstruction, particularly under extremely sparse conditions or in out-of-distribution regimes. To bridge this gap, we propose an architecture-agnostic spatial-physical coupling operator that extends the standard convolution into a joint spatial-variable dimension. Unlike conventional linear channel mixing, our framework constructs a unified spatial-physical representation within CNNs to explicitly capture local inter-variable interactions. By lifting features into a higher-dimensional manifold, this operator significantly enhances the model's representation capacity. Experiments demonstrate that this approach enables strong reconstruction performance and zero-shot generalization, offering a physics-aware inductive bias for super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulence. More broadly, this work suggests that high-dimensional operators offer a promising avenue for modeling intricate multi-scale turbulent flows.

title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
summary: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world contact center applications remains unclear. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that many decision models can match the performance of frontier LLMs on contact center classification, and API-based closed decision models achieve this at the lowest per-request cost among the API models we evaluate. We further observe that their confident predictions are more accurate, enabling selective routing in real-world production scenarios. Across classification tasks, the main weakness of most decision models is abstention: they rarely choose the no-answer option, which accounts for most of their gap to the strongest LLMs (although Gemini-Decision-1 is the notable exception in this regard). We also find that the judging quality of decision models drops sharply for smaller models, and they are also more prone to position bias. In short, our findings provide practical guidance for selecting decision models based on abstention behavior, confidence, and deployment cost, rather than overall accuracy alone.

title: CANDID: Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution in Local Computer-Use Agents
summary: We present CANDID (Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution), an execution-control framework designed to enhance the reliability of local computer-use agents (CUAs) in resource-constrained settings. While local CUAs feature robust baseline proficiency in single-step action prediction, they frequently fail at critical junctions due to rigid action loops or premature DONE decisions. Rather than imposing imprecise cognitive loads through textual reflection, CANDID repurposes parallel test-time scaling into a disciplined, execution-level intervention at sparse, failure-prone points. We introduce a loop-recovery mechanism to filter candidates away from repeated behaviors and a conservative, unanimous DONE gating policy that requires absolute consensus to terminate. Experiments on OSWorld demonstrate that CANDID's structural control significantly improves success rates, outperforming feedback-based alternatives with minimal execution overhead.

title: The Kernel Reality Check: Benchmarking and Distilling Efficient Attention at Scale
summary: Kernelized attention methods, which aim to replace the $O(N^2)$ complexity of softmax attention with $O(N)$ alternatives, have been the focus of intense research in the last five years. Despite growing interest, systematic evaluations and fair comparisons across approaches and scales are still missing. We analyze kernelized attention in two halves and highlight prominent limitations on each. On efficiency, FlashAttention achieves lower memory consumption and faster wall-clock time than SOTA kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths (with inference-time memory in causal language models the only clear exception), contradicting the core assumption for pure kernelized attention used as a drop-in replacement for softmax. We also discover that reported efficiency gains often fail to reproduce against modern baselines. On quality, current kernelized methods leave gaps of 2-10 points relative to softmax under a unified distillation protocol, and model scala alone does not close these gaps. We show this gap is not intrinsic to kernelization: LARA++, a principled extension of LARA that approximates softmax via importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy. We establish that the gap is closable; however, the computational overhead remains substantial, leaving the efficiency wall intact. Code is available at https://github.com/firatoncel/KernelRealityCheckNeurIPS2026

title: LASH-PAT: Deadlock-Free Adaptive Shortest-Path Routing for Inter-Chiplet Interconnects
summary: With the slowdown of transistor scaling, chipletbased systems, and in particular chiplet-based wafer-scale integration, have emerged as a promising approach to sustain growth in computing capability per cost for modern processors and accelerators. In recent years, many specialized inter-chiplet interconnect topologies have been proposed. In these topologies, the simple, well-established, and deadlock-free dimension-order routing scheme is not applicable due to its reliance on regular mesh structures. In this work, we study routing in these recently proposed inter-chiplet interconnect topologies by categorizing and evaluating nine deadlock-free routing functions for irregular topologies known from data center networking in this new context. This reveals a trade-off between turn-based routing, which enables path diversity, and layered routing, which ensures shortest-path delivery. To resolve this trade-off, we propose LASH-PAT, a routing function that extends layered shortestpath routing with adaptive path diversity. LASH-PAT supports multiple shortest paths and dynamically selects among them based on local congestion while preserving deadlock freedom. When compared to the best-performing baseline routing function for each combination of topology, traffic pattern, and evaluated metric, LASH-PAT improves throughput by 21.15% and reduces energy per packet by 12.77%, while providing latency comparable to the lowest-latency baseline routing function.

title: The Shared Word: Evaluating Language Models on Dutch Word Puzzles
summary: Many LLM benchmarks for languages other than English are translated, multiple-choice, or difficult to score automatically. We introduce The Shared Word (TSW-NL), a Dutch benchmark built around four core principles: it is language-specific, open-vocabulary, human-curated, and deterministically scored. Each puzzle gives three clues that describe different senses or uses of the same Dutch word. The clues are individually ambiguous, requiring the solver to combine evidence across multiple clues. We construct the benchmark from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages, followed by automatic filtering and extensive manual curation. The final dataset contains 222 instances, with three independent human answers per test item. The task is clearly challenging: scores in our human study range from 49.5% to 61.0% and the highest-scoring open-weight model we tested reaches only 39.3%. Many others even score below 20%. At the same time, closed-source models show great progress: GPT-4.1 (April 2025) scores 59.2%, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning scores 88.8%. We believe this task provides a useful addition to Dutch model evaluation, plus a clear recipe that can be applied to construct a similar benchmark for other languages.

title: When Do Typed Decision Models Work in Transportation? Evidence from Travel Choice and Traffic Signal Control
summary: Typed decision models combine natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a selected action and an option-level probability distribution without generating lengthy textual responses. Their low inference cost and response latency make them attractive for transportation problems with predefined alternatives. This paper investigates their effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency in two representative transportation tasks: individual travel-mode choice prediction and sequential traffic signal control. We systematically evaluate TypeSafe Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions against conventional transportation methods, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based large language models. Experiments on the Swissmetro dataset show that typed decision models achieve lower prediction accuracy than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline, while their performance varies substantially with input representation and question framing. In closed-loop traffic signal control experiments, typed decision models demonstrate competitive performance against established controllers in several scenarios, but exhibit performance degradation under more challenging network conditions. Furthermore, the typed models achieve lower inference latency and computational cost than the evaluated chat-based large language models, highlighting their potential for efficient, zero-shot transportation decision-making. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of typed decision models, emphasizing the importance of input design, task characteristics, and robustness evaluation for their effective application in transportation systems.

title: Action-outcome coupling: a pre-investment feasibility audit for offline reinforcement learning in supply chain operations
summary: Prescriptive analytics initiatives in logistics, such as offline reinforcement learning and next-best-action systems, are often funded before anyone verifies that the available historical logs can support an improved decision policy. We formalise this pre-investment feasibility question via action-outcome coupling: a total-effect variance index measuring how much expected outcomes change with the logged action. Coupling provides an algorithm-independent upper bound on any policy's achievable value, expressed in monetary units per decision for both single-step and discounted sequential objectives. We also analyse the asymptotic false-licensing risk of an invalid workflow: fitting a value model and evaluating the model's greedy policy on the same data. The false-licence rate is driven mainly by the number of state cells over which selection is performed, rising from the nominal test level with one cell to near certainty with a few dozen, while overlap has a smaller effect. We then propose an audit that assigns logs to four tiers of decision support, separately for fixed and contextual policies, and returns an explicit stopping rationale. On a randomised e-commerce log, the audit endorses a fixed recommendation policy, certifying gains equal to 30 per cent of the theoretical ceiling; the remaining gap reflects bound looseness under an 80-action design. Two public logistics logs fail at different checkpoints: one because the target is an accounting identity of the action, and another because, with 27 clusters, estimated coupling stays below the design's detectability threshold even though a conservative offline learner certifies an improvement in 29 of 30 seeds.

title: Round hyperspheres uniquely minimize most tangent-point energies
summary: We show that round hyperspheres uniquely minimize a broad class of generalized tangent-point energies among all boundaries of bounded Caccioppoli sets sharing the same perimeter or enclosed volume. This includes closed $C^1$-hypersurfaces. Equivalently, we establish sharp lower bounds for the associated scale-invariant ratios of energy to surface measure and energy to volume, respectively, with equality precisely for round spheres.

title: FastSpecFit: Spectrophotometric Modeling of 38 Million Extragalactic Targets from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Second Data Release
summary: Optical spectrophotometry provides a direct window into the physical conditions, kinematics, and formation histories of galaxies and quasars. FastSpecFit is an open-source Python software package that forward-models each Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) spectrum jointly with its broadband photometry, convolving stellar-population synthesis and emission-line templates with each fiber's native spectral resolution. This forward-modeling approach preserves DESI's uncorrelated pixel statistics, fits a typical spectrum in ~0.1 s of single-core time, and scales to tens of millions of objects, with uncertainties estimated via Monte Carlo resampling. FastSpecFit measures stellar velocity dispersions, non-parametric star-formation histories, stellar masses, star-formation rates, dust attenuation, K-corrections, rest-frame magnitudes, and fluxes and equivalent widths for 46 emission lines, including separate narrow and broad components for the Balmer lines. We describe these algorithms in detail, validate the measurements against independent codes, and present the resulting value-added catalog for DESI Data Release 2, which provides spectrophotometric and physical properties for 38 million extragalactic targets at 0<z<4. We also release a companion photometry-only catalog and document the catalogs previously released for the DESI Early Data Release and Data Release 1.

title: Prioritize, Don't Decide: What We Learned Auditing a Deployed Human-in-the-Loop CV Sorter
summary: A single academic vacancy can draw hundreds of applications, and the first screening round consumes most of a committee's time. We describe a CV Priority Sorter deployed at a national platform for academic vacancies and integrated with its vacancy database. It proposes a reading order for a pile of CVs and leaves every decision to the committee, pairing a frozen multilingual transformer encoder with a per-session linear model that retrains after each label and is discarded when the session ends. It works: on a pool of 300 synthetic CVs, a committee reading in the tool's order reaches 95% of the relevant candidates after half the pile, where an arbitrary order needs almost all of it. This paper is about what we found when we audited that claim, rather than about the system itself. Three findings changed the product. The pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, which makes precision-style metrics on it uninformative; regenerating it under a shared length budget removes that shortcut and leaves the reading-depth result standing. The four-level agreement score such systems report, ours included, is a binary probability cut at fixed thresholds, so it follows the classifier's confidence rather than its ranking and falls as labels accumulate. And uncertainty sampling, the obvious way to implement a "suggest the next CV" button, leaves model quality intact but raises the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline, because the CVs it asks about are the ones that would otherwise be skipped. A fourth result shows where to look next: a hosted LLM embedding model lifts zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80 under length control, then stops mattering once the session model has two dozen labels; a local cross-encoder matches that cold-start gain without sending data out. We report the fixes each finding forced.

title: Arboreus: A Realistic Boreal Forest Simulator with Topographic Terrain and Satellite-Informed Parametric Tree Distributions
summary: This work presents Arboreus, a realistic Boreal forest simulator, developed to support statistical validation of robotic autonomy algorithms in Boreal forest environments. Arboreus presents an automated methodology for synthesizing large-scale, data-informed, plausible forest worlds from parametric trees, height-variant terrain, and satellite-informed tree density distributions. The parametric generation of dominant Boreal tree species such as Birch, Spruce, and Pine is guided by trunk, canopy, and foliage parameters, extracted from growth studies in the Nordic areas. Tree distribution in an area of interest is guided by the Copernicus satellite dataset, which provides tree cover density and dominant species type at up to 10m raster resolution. The forest floor generation is guided by topographic data from the Swedish cadastral agency to produce realistic data-informed terrains. Given coordinates and extents of forested areas of interest, Arboreus synthesizes data-informed plausible forests, while offering flexibility to inject user observations of real forests (detail, age, dimensionality and tree count), which is critical for realistic synthetic data generation and for the testing of feature-sensitive autonomy algorithms. The applicability of Arboreus for benchmarking and validation of robot autonomy for different robot mobilities is demonstrated in Gazebosim, Unreal Engine, and Isaac Sim physics engines. The applicability of Arboreus as a source of synthetic forest data and its potential to support downstream forest resource mapping research (volume estimation, tree instance segmentation and stem attribute estimation) is also demonstrated. Arboreus has been open-sourced along with a dataset comprising 25 Boreal forest worlds of size 1000m2 corresponding to three real forest sites.

title: Think Before You Code: A Benchmark for Testing LLMs on Software Engineering Deliberation
summary: Think Before You Code (TBYC) is a benchmark pipeline for studying whether code-focused language models can reason about software issues in ways that resemble human engineering deliberation. The benchmark curates GitHub issue discussions into structured records, extracts human discussion artifacts such as problems, solutions, constraints, rationales, and trade-offs, and then prompts models to generate issue-level "thoughts" using retrieved code context and few-shot examples. It converts model responses back into the same artifact space and evaluates them against human annotations using complementary metrics for artifact type detection, metadata matching, tag overlap, and semantic summary similarity. Beyond scoring, this study includes visualization, leaderboard, and baseline tools that make it possible to compare models, prompting strategies, and extraction methods across repositories and issues. Think Before You Code is an end-to-end evaluation environment for measuring how closely LLM software reasoning aligns with human strategic judgment.

title: BRepA: Graph-Based B-Rep Pretraining for Unified CAD Understanding and Generation
summary: Boundary representation (B-Rep) of CAD models encodes geometric primitives and their relations as a graph structure, enabling efficient shape modeling within CAD software. Learning on B-Reps for downstream tasks, such as segmentation and novel shape generation, requires specialized neural network designs. Moreover, performance improvements and accelerated training can be achieved with effective pretraining strategies, which is particularly important for tasks with limited labeled B-Rep data. In this paper, we introduce BRepA, a unified self-supervised pretraining framework that explicitly reconstructs both the geometry and topology of B-Rep objects via graph-based modeling. By learning from large-scale unlabeled CAD data only once, BRepA produces representations that generalize across tasks and significantly enhance both discriminative and generative learning. On segmentation tasks, BRepA demonstrates remarkable data efficiency. For instance, with only 1% labeled samples, BRepA pretraining improves mIoU by 32.52% compared to models trained from scratch. On generative tasks, aligning diffusion model representations with pretrained BRepA features substantially accelerates convergence, achieving nearly 2 times faster training while improving generation quality under the same computational budget, despite the diffusion model being roughly 20 times larger than BRepA. Overall, our results show that geometry- and topology-aware B-Rep pretraining provides a powerful foundation for both understanding and generating CAD structures, serving as a versatile representation backbone for diverse downstream applications. We will release the code to facilitate future research.

title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
summary: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).

title: You Only Encode Once: Sub-Pixel-Shifted Frames for Arbitrary-Scale Remote Sensing Super-Resolution with 2D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Arbitrary-scale super-resolution (ASSR) of remote sensing images remains challenging due to the limited high-frequency information in a single low-resolution (LR) observation. While multi-frame SR can exploit complementary sub-pixel information, existing approaches often require real multi-frame training sequences and repeated feature encoding, increasing data acquisition demands and computational costs. To address these limitations, we propose SPS-GS (Sub-Pixel-Shifted Gaussian Splatting), an encode-once framework that learns from multi-phase LR observations synthesized from individual high-resolution images, without requiring real multi-frame training sequences. Specifically, Phase-Coherent Aliasing Demodulation (PCAD) exploits shift-dependent aliasing through Fourier-based alignment, phase-aware residual fusion, and least-squares aliasing estimation, enabling multi-frame information to be integrated before a single deep encoding pass. Gaussian Projection Alignment (GPA) then iteratively refines Gaussian centers and colors using multi-observation back-projection to promote observation consistency. The refined Gaussians support continuous rendering at arbitrary scales. Extensive experiments on five remote sensing datasets demonstrate strong reconstruction performance against single-image and multi-frame SR baselines, while maintaining competitive inference efficiency at common scales. The code will be publicly released.

title: Impact of Pretraining Length, Model Size, and Annotation Budget on Downstream Clinical Tasks of Foundation Models in Radiotherapy
summary: Cone-beam CT (CBCT) scans acquired during radiotherapy capture changes such as tumor shrinkage and radiation-induced tissue changes, offering great potential for foundation models that help monitor individual treatment responses. However, to our knowledge, no large-scale pretrained models for radiotherapy CBCT exist, and evaluating modeling choices is difficult since downstream tasks are not known in advance. We examine how pretraining length, model size, and finetuning strategy relate to downstream clinical performance, and how metrics tracked during pretraining correlate with it. We pretrain vision transformer encoders with masked image modeling on about 150,000 raw 3D radiotherapy CBCT scans, tracking representation quality via validation loss, effective rank, and linear probing. Downstream tasks are classification of feeding tube presence ($n=51,135$ CBCTs, $1,562$ patients) and clinical characteristics (T-, N-stage, sex, age, tumor site; $n=1,278$ patients) in head and neck cancer. We compare low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and full finetuning against no pretraining, varying annotated dataset size. Pretext validation loss was the most consistent predictor of downstream performance; effective rank and linear probing were also associated, but not consistently across model sizes and finetuning methods. LoRA performed comparably to full finetuning while training only 0.5-2.5% of the parameters. Fully finetuned models consistently outperformed models without pretraining across all sizes, with AUROC 0.91-0.97 vs. 0.58-0.85 for feeding tube classification and 0.99-1.00 vs. 0.71-0.97 for sex classification. Model size had only a small, inconsistent effect, suggesting smaller models suffice at lower computational cost. Code and pretrained models (non-commercial license): https://github.com/alexCortinaU/RT-CBCT_SSL

title: Wear and Go: Calibration Free Sparse Inertial Motion Capture via Online Sensor Setup Estimation
summary: Sparse inertial motion capture typically assumes that each sensor's anatomical identity and mounting orientation are known. We present MOSAIC (Motion-based Sensor Assignment and Inertial Calibration), a framework that recovers this setup from ordinary motion without a calibration pose. Our central insight is that body pose changes continuously while the sensor setup persists, allowing movements that are individually ambiguous to provide complementary evidence over time. A setup network processes unordered sensor streams with temporal and cross-sensor attention, then accumulates assignment and rotation evidence into a session-level estimate. The recovered setup canonicalizes measurements for frozen pretrained pose estimators, separating sensor configuration from motion reconstruction. For sensors worn at prescribed body sites, evaluation on real inertial recordings with randomized setups shows near-calibrated pose accuracy for bounded offsets and substantial benefits from accumulation under arbitrary orientations. Transfer across pose networks supports setup recovery as a reusable interface between interchangeable sensors and pretrained pose models.

title: Scalar inelastic scattering of pseudo-Majorana dark matter through a radion portal
summary: We investigate a radion portal for pseudo-Majorana dark matter as an interpretation of the high-recoil event LZ230616. In contrast to the familiar pseudo-Dirac regime, the pseudo-Majorana structure allows a dominant scalar transition while suppressing elastic scattering. Endothermic kinematics remove low-energy recoils, while the nuclear response shapes the surviving high-recoil spectrum. Combining the accepted LZ event count with the Born-level thermal relic abundance yields a reference solution with $m_χ=1$ TeV, $δ=340$ keV, and $m_r=30$ GeV. This solution lies within the published LZ spin-independent $\mathcal{O}_1^s$ interval and remains compatible with existing OPAL and CMS constraints, while a simplified HL-LHC diphoton projection could probe it. Solar neutrino searches offer a complementary test. The benchmark's energetic-daughter proxy rates are comparable in magnitude to the rate scales reconstructed from IceCube's direct $b\bar{b}$ and $τ^+τ^-$ templates. An illustrative IceCube-Gen2 rescaling suggests future sensitivity, while a model-specific assessment requires the radion-cascade neutrino spectra and detector response.

title: Beyond Attribute-Centric Fairness: Modelling and Mitigating Unified Bias Representation in Omni-modal Large Language Models
summary: Omni-modal large language models (OLLMs) provide joint multimodal understanding and generation capabilities, making them well-suited to complex environments and promising backbones for next-generation AI. Despite these advances, the harmful stereotypes encoded in such models manifest in increasingly diverse forms, leading to broader and more severe societal consequences. Existing debiasing methods typically impose separate fairness objectives for each sensitive attribute and modality to minimise demographic-dependent variations. However, in omni-modal settings, this attribute-centric paradigm struggles to jointly address diverse social biases with distinct fairness objectives and to generalise beyond predefined attributes. To this end, we propose OmniDebias, one of the first methods for promoting fairness in OLLMs, which employs a bias-centric formulation to extract and mitigate a shared bias representation across attributes and modalities while preserving attribute-related knowledge. Specifically, we exploit activation inconsistencies of a given attribute (e.g., gender) across semantic contexts (e.g., occupations) to disentangle bias from legitimate knowledge. We further consolidate multiple extracted biases into a shared representation, formulating a unified objective that captures the underlying structure across social biases and generalises to unseen attributes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that eliminating unified bias with both post-hoc editing and fine-tuning can consistently improve fairness across diverse attributes and modalities in OLLMs while maintaining favourable utility.

title: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation
summary: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. Sequential test-time scaling can improve exploitation performance, but larger budgets do not ensure sustained exploration: agents often stop with budget remaining. Yet what happens when execution continues beyond stopping remains underexplored. We investigate this gap on ExploitBench using DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. We find additional verified gains after the first stop response, but gains diminish over longer execution. We identify two patterns associated with less productive continuation: an increasing proportion of stop responses within the same context and earlier stopping associated with summaries retaining impossibility judgments about unachieved capabilities. To test whether context management can elicit further capability, we propose SCoRe, which compacts context at stop bursts and marks these judgments as unproven. SCoRe improves verified capability over summary-based continuation and other evaluated context-management baselines. With SCoRe, MiMo reaches a capability coverage score of 67.0% at 2,000 turns, exceeding both 32.4% under the original stopping policy and the 58.6% computed for GPT-5.5 from ExploitBench's 300-turn reference results on the same tasks. These findings show that stopping need not mark an agent's exploitation limit, and that continued execution with context management can elicit substantial further capability.

title: Euclid: Quick Data Release (Q1) -- The evolution of the radio-loud AGN fraction-stellar mass relation to $z\sim3$ in the Euclid Deep Field North
summary: The incidence of radio-loud active galactic nuclei (RLAGN) and their energetic output via AGN feedback are crucial in understanding the evolution of galaxies and the large-scale structure of the Universe. In the local Universe, the incidence of RLAGN has been shown to correlate strongly with host galaxy properties, particularly stellar mass. Using the large-area survey capabilities provided by Euclid and the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), we present the first study of the RLAGN incidence--stellar mass relation to $z=3.0$. We perform a stringent analysis accounting for cross-matching reliability and stellar-mass incompleteness. In addition, we test the robustness of our results against AGN and host galaxy classification. This yields a sample of $3\,154$ RLAGN in the Euclid Deep Field North, comprising $2\,803$ low-excitation radio galaxies (LERGs). We find that the LERG incidence as a function of stellar mass and radio luminosity follows a tight correlation over more than two orders of magnitude in stellar mass to $z=3.0$. The slope of the power-law relation decreases from $γ\approx2.5$ in the local Universe to $γ\approx1.0$ at $z=3.0$, indicating a relative increase in low-mass LERGs at earlier epochs. Separating the LERG population into actively star-forming and quiescent galaxies reveals that quiescent LERGs show a much steeper relation between incidence and stellar mass, with $γ\approx2.5$ compared to star-forming LERGs that show $γ\approx1.5$. However, the relation seems to be independent of whether galaxies are star-forming or quiescent at $z\geq2$, where both populations show relatively flat relations with $γ\approx1.0$. Our results suggest an evolutionary picture in which the LERG population transitions from cold-mode, merger-dominated accretion at earlier epochs to a scenario in which systems require a massive hot halo to fuel the AGN in the local Universe.

title: RoadAnnoter: An AI-Assisted Desktop Tool for Semantic Segmentation Annotation of Road-Scene Images
summary: Accurate semantic segmentation of road-scene images is essential for road safety research; however, polygon-level annotation remains labor-intensive and limits labelled dataset development. This study presents RoadAnnoter v1.0, an open-source desktop application integrating six human-in-the-loop annotation modes: manual polygon delineation, SAM Prompt, Smart Select, Edge Fill, pretrained semantic segmentation using Cityscapes-trained SegFormer models, and task-specific segmentation using TinySegNet, a lightweight MobileNetV3-Small-based network trained with accumulated annotator-generated labels. SAM-based modes use promptable segmentation with SAM and MobileSAM, while Edge Fill combines Canny edge detection with colour-similarity-based flood filling in CIELAB colour space. SegFormer generates suggestions for common road-scene categories, whereas TinySegNet supports adaptation to project-specific features through iterative training. All six modes use a shared mask-to-polygon pipeline comprising morphological processing, Gaussian smoothing, contour extraction, and Douglas-Peucker simplification; annotations are exported in YOLO segmentation format. RoadAnnoter was used to annotate Google Street View images from recorded road accident locations in Bangladesh for a vision-language model-based investigation of free-flow speed estimation. Qualitative assessment across representative scenes demonstrated the complementary applicability of the annotation modes to diverse feature geometries. Visual comparison with Roboflow indicated similar qualitative boundary characteristics for principal road-scene regions, although no quantitative accuracy assessment was conducted. RoadAnnoter provides a locally operated framework for developing road-scene segmentation datasets for transportation engineering and road safety research.

title: Learning Agent-Centric Vision-Language-Action World Models for Autonomous Driving
summary: Recent progress in integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models with world modeling has significantly advanced end-to-end autonomous driving by allowing systems to reason about imagined futures instead of merely reacting to current observations. However, most world VLA models generate future frames at the pixel level with plenty of dense visual tokens. Although such generated futures can be visually plausible, they preserve many driving-irrelevant appearance details, i.e., only a small portion of the tokens directly encode critical planning-relevant factors, such as agent geometry, motion dynamics, and interactions. This introduces a significant performance bottleneck. An important question thus arises: what world state should a world VLA model reason over to support planning beyond pixel-level prediction? We argue that planning-oriented world modeling should focus on a compact and structured agent-centric latent state that captures the interactions between objects in the driving scene over time. As such, we introduce AgentWorld, an agent-centric VLA world model that uses discrete agent tokens jointly for reasoning and trajectory planning. Each token is dynamically grounded to a surrounding agent associated with its object's state, such as semantic identity, 3D geometry, motion, and interaction context. AgentWorld learns these tokens through three key processes: explicit geometric grounding, reasoning-oriented supervised fine-tuning, and agent-oriented reinforcement learning. Extensive open-loop and closed-loop experiments under diverse driving scenarios show that AgentWorld enhances planning capabilities, fully exploits visual evidence and agent dynamics, and yields interpretable agent-centric world states.

title: Outcome-Balanced PPO and Policy-Induced Flow Rectification for Flow-Based VLA Policies
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables post-training of flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies by optimizing expected task return through environment interaction. However, this optimization raises two challenges: policy updates can alter the velocity-field geometry underlying the score approximation used for stochastic transitions, and sparse multi-task rollouts can yield uneven learning signals across tasks and advantage signs. We introduce an RL framework that combines Outcome-Balanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with policy-induced flow rectification. Outcome-Balanced PPO reweights positive advantages using task success-rate estimates and rescales positive and negative advantages while preserving their signs. Policy-induced rectification periodically fits a linear-bridge flow to ODE endpoint pairs generated by the current policy, refreshing the representation used in subsequent stochastic optimization. We evaluate the framework on simulated manipulation benchmarks and additionally study a component combination in a Real2Sim2Real task, examining task performance, optimization behavior, and flow consistency. The proposed framework improves success rates over the evaluated baselines across the simulated benchmarks.

title: Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance
summary: Learned super-resolution of physical fields must satisfy structural constraints---such as divergence-free flow ($\nabla\cdot u=0$), curl-free fields ($\nabla\times u=0$), and pointwise sum-to-one normalization ($1^\top p=1$)---that standard training objectives do not enforce. Soft penalties trade fidelity against satisfaction via a scalar hyperparameter $λ$ but cannot drive the residual to zero; hard-constrained regression eliminates the residual by construction yet converges to the conditional mean, losing small-scale spectral structure. We observe that in Conditional Flow Matching with linear paths, a linear constraint $Ax=c$ is preserved along the entire transport trajectory whenever the velocity field is compatible ($Av_θ=0$) and the initial noise is consistent ($Ax_0=c$); along the trajectory, the latter two conditions are also necessary. We term this the path-equivariance principle and instantiate it in PACE (Path-Aligned Constraint Equivariance), a framework that enforces these conditions through a null-space parameterization of the velocity field and a constraint-respecting noise sampler, with no modification to the loss function or the ODE integrator. Across three constraint families, PACE reduces the mean constraint residual by one to five orders of magnitude relative to unconstrained baselines, matching the residual level of the data-generation pipeline itself. The proposed framework requires only a closed-form parameterization onto the null space of $A$; within this scope, it offers exact constraint enforcement while recovering the spectral content and predictive diversity that conditional-mean regression systematically loses, all under a single unified recipe.

title: Engineering antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices
summary: In this study, we demonstrate the atomic-scale engineering of antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices grown by MBE on (001)-oriented SrTiO3 substrates. Our work achieved a precise layer-by-layer control, revealing how interface-driven structural distortions can be systematically tuned. X-ray diffraction and reciprocal space mapping confirm both the epitaxial strain state and the high crystalline quality of the superlattices. High-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy further uncovers layer-resolved atomic displacements, where La3+ and Pr3+ exhibit antipolar motions modulated by the superlattice periodicity. The alternate stackings of LaVO3 and PrVO3 yield a unique antiferromagnetic transition temperature, which can be tuned by adjusting their relative proportions. This behavior exists despite the distinct spin ordering temperatures observed in the constituent materials. Layer-resolved spectroscopic measurements reveal that the hybridization of La and Pr 5d orbitals with O 2p orbitals is also modulated and directly correlated to the oxygen octahedra rotations. By determining the orbital hybridization and mapping the cation displacements as proxies, we can visualize indirectly the trilinear coupling between oxygen octahedra rotations and antipolar rare earth displacements. Notably, the interfacial oxygen octahedra connectivity between cubic SrTiO3 substrate and orthorhombic vanadate layers significantly influences the structural distortions. These distortions, almost quenched near the interface, relax over few unit cells, demonstrating how strain and interfacial effects propagate through the superlattice. This study illustrates how artificial superlattices can be engineered to control structural distortions at the atomic scale, offering a pathway to tune the magnetic properties through strain-distortion relationships in perovskite oxides.

title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops
summary: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.

title: Better Rankers, Worse Retrievers: The Hidden Cost of RL Post-Training in Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommenders decode the semantic ID of a user's next item with a language model, and post-training them with reinforcement learning (RL) after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become standard practice. The gains are mostly reported on the first ten results, yet in deployment such models hand hundreds of candidates to a downstream ranker or reward model. We show that RL post-training has a hidden cost: it improves accuracy at the top of the list (hit@K for small K) but, on all five datasets we study, lowers the recall of the candidate list (hit@K for K in the hundreds). The model becomes a better ranker and a worse retriever. Controlled experiments trace the loss to the negative advantages that RL assigns to the candidates it samples, the rollout. The root cause is that only one next item is logged per user, so RL treats every other candidate as wrong. Yet these candidates are the model's most plausible alternatives, and often the next items of other users with similar histories. Penalising them pushes down exactly what similar users choose next, and these items drop out of those users' candidate lists. This diagnosis points directly to a remedy: out-of-rollout anchoring, a single additional loss term that preserves the SFT model's ordering of the items outside the rollout. It keeps the gain at the top and restores recall to the SFT level on all five datasets, and it is effective under other RL configurations as well. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of this recall loss: we measure it, identify its cause, and show that, once the cause is known, a simple remedy suffices.

title: A Survey on RLOps for Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become increasingly important for improving the reasoning, instruction-following, and task-solving capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, scaling RL training exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that can waste computational resources, slow training, and undermine model improvements. These challenges have motivated a growing body of techniques for LLM RLOps, which manages the efficiency and reliability of operations throughout the LLM reinforcement learning training lifecycle. Despite growing interest, these techniques remain scattered across research areas, with limited synthesis of their operational roles and interactions. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of LLM RLOps methods. We organize existing approaches into five stages: Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation. Within each stage, we examine operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence. Building on this taxonomy, we identify open challenges and future directions in training process observability, cross-stage coordination, generalizable RLOps, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement. These directions extend operational management from individual training runs to diverse training settings, shared infrastructure, and successive improvement cycles. We maintain a GitHub repository indexing relevant papers and open resources at https://github.com/zhanglingzhe0820/Awesome-RLOps.

title: TabDAG: Structured Evolutionary Search for Tabular Feature Engineering
summary: Feature engineering can improve tabular prediction, but useful transformations are compositional, data-dependent, and subject to leakage constraints. We present TabDAG, a framework that combines evolutionary search with a graph representation of feature-engineering programs. Nodes implement row-wise or data-fitted transformations; edges encode dependencies among raw variables, intermediate values, and final features. The representation supports interactions, statistical encodings, clustering- and neighborhood-based features, and multi-stage compositions in a single executable program. Mutations are structured edits constrained by a parent-specific schema and checked before evaluation. In our experiments, no structurally invalid program reached evaluation, although proposals could be rejected and valid graphs could still fail at runtime. Across ten regression and classification datasets and three tabular model families, evolved features improve predictive performance over raw inputs. TabDAG and its combination with OpenFE achieve the two best mean ranks among the compared methods; pairwise rank differences between feature-engineering methods do not survive multiple-testing correction. The LLM-based searches use the same backbone and candidate-evaluation budget. A controlled ablation compares free-form Python, whole-graph JSON, and constrained graph edits with the search engine, budget, and backbone held fixed. Constrained edits yield fewer failed evaluations than either rewrite baseline. The resulting graphs expose the transformations and dependencies selected by search, enabling feature-level analysis of the observed gains.

title: Compact and Decodable Electrocardiogram Text for Large Language Models
summary: When a twelve-lead electrocardiogram is written as text for a large language model, the number of tokens has to be balanced against the information lost through compression. This paper presents a deterministic encoding that writes eight independent leads as amplitude letters and exact time gaps and recovers the remaining four limb leads algebraically. The key points are selected with a cardiac-cycle-dependent tolerance, the amplitudes are parameterized by a 26-letter logarithmic codebook learned from a training set, and a 10-step tolerance schedule keeps all records within a fixed token budget. The encoding was applied to 21,388 records from the public PTB-XL database and evaluated using an exact decode-and-re-encode round trip, waveform reconstruction error, and a paired comparison of convolutional classifiers trained with 5 different seeds on signals from the original and decoded databases. All records were contained in 4,080 tokens (average: 2,866 tokens, 64.3% fewer than a per-sample transcription), and all stored lead strings were exactly reproduced. The average correlation between the decoded and reference signals was 0.982. The macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.9167 for the reference signals and 0.9157 for the decoded signals (paired difference -0.0010; 95% patient-level bootstrap interval, -0.0028 to 0.0007), within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of -0.010; this is not a confirmatory result, because the test fold had been used during encoder development. The diagnostic content of a compact text can therefore be preserved, while the language model's ability to read the text is yet another matter.

title: Theta-Eta Mellin Transforms, Shifted Reflections, and Rigorous Approximation Theory for a Variant Theta Construction
summary: We develop a rigorous analytic framework for investigating a proposed functional equation associated with a variant theta construction. We prove the classical Mellin identity connecting the Jacobi kernel $1-θ_4(0\mid ix^2)$ to the completed Dirichlet eta function, and extend its Mellin transform meromorphically to the whole plane with a single simple pole at the origin. Mellin uniqueness identifies $x^{3/8}(1-θ_4(0\mid ix^2))$ as the unique kernel in a natural weighted $L^1$ class whose Mellin transform is the shifted completed eta function. We distinguish this Gaussian kernel from the weighted exponential series $Θ^B(s)=\sum_{n\geq1}ne^{-ns}$, whose Mellin transform is $Γ(s)ζ(s-1)$ and obeys a different, explicitly derived reflection relation. We show that every affine reflection $s\mapsto c-s$ can be generated for a shifted completed eta or zeta function by choosing the shift appropriately; consequently, the occurrence of $\tfrac14-s$ alone cannot identify the original variant with a shifted eta function. The corrected analytic product defined here is an elementary meromorphic multiplier of the completed zeta function and therefore has a precise $1-s$ functional equation. We prove an explicit eta-tail bound, a sharper alternating-tail asymptotic, a uniformly convergent Euler-transformed eta series with a geometric error bound, a uniform zeta-approximation bound away from the line $\Re s=1$, and a combined truncation estimate when both the zeta and weighted-exponential factors are truncated. We also determine the principal Laurent data and the cancellation of the gamma poles at the trivial zeta zeros for the corrected product. Reproducible high-precision experiments verify the stated error scales. The exact identification of the original variant with a shifted completed eta function remains open.

title: Pixel is All You Need
summary: Text, images, audio, touch, and even robot actions can, in principle, all be rendered onto a single canvas, suggesting an ambitious goal of unifying all modalities within vision. Language provides the natural first test. To subsume it, a visual model must reason directly over text in pixels. Across a wide range of image, video, and unified multimodal generators, however, we find that their visual generation modules cannot perform symbolic reasoning over text on the canvas. They succeed only when an underlying text module or prompt rewriter already supplies the answer, effectively reducing the generator to a mere renderer, a limitation that post-training does little to resolve. To test whether this failure stems from pixels themselves or from current training paradigms, we train a family of purely pixel-space generative models from scratch without any text pathway. With images as their sole input and output, these models read questions, write intermediate steps, and produce answers directly on the canvas. Remarkably, they exhibit hallmark behaviors of large language models. Performance improves predictably with scale following a power law. Writing intermediate steps frame by frame substantially outperforms single-frame answering, echoing chain-of-thought, while reinforcement-learning post-training further strengthens reasoning. Moreover, sharing one canvas allows the same model to reason across modalities, a capability that text-only language models lack. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of these phenomena in purely pixel-space generative models free of text tokens.

title: Where Do Highly Cited Scientists Stand? A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Positional Distribution in the Top 2% Ranking
summary: The Top 2% Scientists list is widely used. Yet current applications either only count the number of scientists in different units or criticize the list's validity as a measure of individual impact. We introduce positional enrichment, a scale-free framework that compares observed to expected counts across percentile bins on the list, revealing where a unit's scientists tend to sit along the list rather than how many it contributes. Applying positional enrichment to the 2026 single-year list, we show that countries, institutions, and research subfields each fall into a consistent pattern of three groups with Head-, Middle-, and Tail-enriched profiles. Subfield profiles are globally stable, whereas countries and institutions are heterogeneous across subfields. National and institutional differences are therefore compositional. Therefore, the reason of a country or institution sitting near the head of the list is unlikely its scientists performing better within the same subfields, while it holding more of the subfields that sit near the head. Academic age adds an independent dimension, with stronger enrichment toward the head after 25 years and exceptions in fast-moving subfields such as artificial intelligence. We show the ranking is not a flat ordering of individual influence but a subfield-organized stratification.

title: Pluggable Subband-Decoupled Fusion and Unlabeled Capture Prototype Calibration: Bridging High-SNR Null-Subcarrier Regrowth and Low-SNR Coherent Preambles for Cross-Domain IoT RF Fingerprinting
summary: Zero-overhead physical-layer authentication at edge wireless access points (APs) is vital for securing resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) transceivers against credential cloning, yet cross-domain IEEE 802.11a/g radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) faces an acute signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) crossover. Power-amplifier spectral regrowth on unpopulated null subcarriers resists indoor multipath at high SNR but decays quadratically below the thermal noise floor, whereas populated active in-band preambles survive low SNR yet degrade under severe multipath, causing static fusion to lose up to 44.7 percentage points (pp). To our knowledge, we propose the first RFFI framework that dynamically modulates active in-band waveforms and unpopulated null-subcarrier regrowth via a blind physical SNR gate: Pluggable Gated Subband-Decoupled Fusion with Unlabeled Capture-Aware Prototype Calibration (GSDF-CAPC). Avoiding the 20-35 dB subband gradient imbalance of joint training, GSDF pairs any frozen pretrained host backbone with a 46.3K null-subcarrier plug-in encoder (NS-Branch), fusing scale-standardized logits and gate-warped spherical embeddings under a source-calibrated lag-64 thermal-SNR gate with exact low-SNR fallback. Over unlabeled target AP captures, forward-only unbalanced optimal-transport calibration (UOT-CAPC) aligns shifted prototypes under packet-arrival skew and recovers parameter-free balanced Sinkhorn (U-CAPC) at equipartition. Across DataPort-WiFi, WiSig, and ORBIT MobRFFI, zero-retrain GSDF wins all 72/72 paired runs across eight backbones with 0.00 pp low-SNR loss, while edge IB-Host + GSDF (92.6K-93.3K active parameters, 1.82 ms single-core CPU latency) and timing-synchronized GSDF-STO / GSDF-Tri reach 57.50%-65.05% three-benchmark Macro-F1 (89.04%-100.00% over 5-10-packet IoT bursts).

title: DOOM-GS: Dynamic Out-of-core Optimization for Massive Gaussian Splatting
summary: Traditional Gaussian Splatting (GS) methods use in-core training, i.e. assuming that GPU memory is large enough to accommodate all the primitives. This assumption breaks down when the primitives exceed the capacity of GPU memory, e.g. GS on large environments. Recent out-of-core training research starts to address this issue, but is limited to static scenes. Unlike static GS, dynamic GS primitives move in space and time, breaking common assumptions held in existing out-of-core research and impose new challenges in memory management and training. To this end, we propose Dynamic Out-of-core Optimization for Massive Gaussian Splatting (DOOM-GS), the first out-of-core optimization method designed specifically for massive-scale dynamic GS. DOOM-GS is equipped with novel memory management strategies that optimize caching for spatio-temporal primitives, and a fast learning method for large numbers of primitives. Due to the lack of suitable datasets for large-scale dynamic GS, we also contribute a new dataset for evaluation. Since there are no directly comparable methods, we adapt several closely related methods for comparison. Through extensive evaluation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of DOOM-GS which now makes it possible to reconstruct city-scale dynamic scenes with high quality on moderate hardware, serving as a foundational tool for diverse future research and applications.

title: Improving On-board Shape Models Using Sun Sensors and Implicit Representations
summary: We propose an original, end-to-end approach to generate and refine the onboard 3D shape model of irregular small bodies, such as asteroids, using only low-cost Sun sensor eclipse data and coarse a priori knowledge, tailored for resource-constrained missions like CubeSats. Leveraging EclipseNets, a differentiable neural model of eclipse boundaries, our pipeline first refines 2D silhouettes by learning from real-time entry and exit events during spacecraft orbits, avoiding the limitations of traditional imaging or lidar in bandwidth-starved environments. These silhouettes then supervise a compact neural signed-distance field with periodic activations, enabling incremental updates to a high-fidelity implicit geometry representation capable of capturing fine-scale features and concavities. In simulations of the body Eros under realistic orbital dynamics, the method increases silhouette IoU from 0.70 to 0.87 and produces coherent 3D reconstructions, suggesting our approach could find a place in future autonomous architectures for small-body exploration.

title: Global rigidity and the Hessian energy identity for the one-phase Bernoulli problem
summary: We prove that every entire classical stable solution of the one-phase Bernoulli problem in dimension five or six is one-dimensional. In dimensions three through six, we establish an exact interior identity for the scale-invariant Hessian energy of sequences with bounded Morse index. Hence, the global stability conjecture is solved.

title: Greedy Empirical Bayes for Density Estimation
summary: Bayesian nonparametric density estimation is challenging in high dimensions, where traditional approaches like the Dirichlet process (DP) mixture rely on computationally intensive Markov chain Monte Carlo or approximations. We introduce the partition posterior bootstrap (PPB), where a flexible prior is constructed by smoothing a DP over a partition of the sample space. Conditioned on this partition, exact posterior sampling reduces to a simple Bayesian bootstrap-like algorithm. Importantly, we select the partition using a greedy empirical Bayes (GEB) algorithm which scales to high dimensions and large sample sizes. GEB greedily maximizes the closed-form marginal likelihood via local split decisions arising naturally from its factorization, yielding an adaptive binary tree partition. Our key theoretical result is that the GEB tree belongs to an admissible family with high probability, splitting all identifiable signals while avoiding over-splitting noise. As a result, the PPB posterior with the GEB tree attains adaptive contraction rates. Our theory holds under weak, verifiable assumptions, which we demonstrate in numerous examples. Empirically, PPB delivers accurate density estimates and uncertainty quantification at a fraction of the computational cost of other approaches, making it a practical off-the-shelf choice for high-dimensional Bayesian density estimation with theoretical guarantees.

title: IntentGR: Enhancing Intent for End-to-End Personalized Generative Retrieval in Search
summary: Personalized generative retrieval in search should jointly satisfy the user's immediate search intent and long-term preference. Recent end-to-end approaches, primarily explored in recommendation, unify item tokenization and sequence generation within a single model, allowing semantic identifiers (SIDs) to be optimized toward the downstream generation objective. However, these methods often treat the query merely as an input feature, without explicitly leveraging it to guide either identifier learning or sequence generation. This leaves intent guidance weak in both the tokenization and the generation stage, causing generated semantic identifiers to drift toward high-frequency token patterns rather than the current search intent. In this work, we find that incorporating additional query-related evidence into the framework of end-to-end generative retrieval is important. Based on this finding, we propose IntentGR, an intent-enhanced end-to-end framework that strengthens query semantics at four complementary stages of the retrieval pipeline. Query-Aware Semantic Behavior Representation (QBR) introduces query-level behavioral evidence as a new input signal; Query-Semantic Alignment (QSA), Long-Tail Query Enrichment (LQE), and Query-conditioned Attention Modulation (QAM) then serve as integration mechanisms at the optimization, training-distribution, and decoding stages to fully exploit this evidence. Experiments on the public AOL4PS benchmark and AE, a large-scale industrial e-commerce dataset, show that IntentGR improves Recall@10 by 8.11% and 11.96% over the strongest baseline, with strong gains on long-tail queries. These results suggest that enriched query-related input evidence, together with effective integration mechanisms, is beneficial for building intent-aware end-to-end generative search systems.

title: PANO: Parallel Latent Space Neural Operator for Solving PDEs
summary: Aggregating observations into a limited number of latent tokens and learning physical interactions in the latent space has emerged as an effective approach for Transformer-based neural operators to solve Partial Differential Equation (PDE) problems involving large-scale observations. However, existing methods typically compress observations using a single aggregation pattern, making physical information not retained by that pattern invisible to the latent space and thereby constraining physical interactions within it. To address this limitation, we propose PArallel Latent Space Neural Operator (PANO), a novel neural operator for solving PDEs that formulates physical interactions among observations as an additive combination of interaction results from parallel latent spaces with shared parameters. Specifically, PANO transforms observations into multiple distinct compressed representations through independent mappings, learns physical interactions in parallel based on these representations, and finally fuses the decoded results to predict the target physical field. Within PANO, we further propose Coupled Assignment Projection (CAP) to construct bidirectionally consistent encoding and decoding mappings, and Pairwise Latent Space Attention Layer (PaLA) to jointly update latent representations of each latent space through adaptive cross-space interactions. Extensive experiments on nine benchmarks spanning diverse physical systems, geometries, and observation scales demonstrate that PANO achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, PANO reduces equivalent plastic strain prediction errors on Unilateral Stamping by 28.3% (or more) and lift-coefficient prediction errors on AirCraft by 21.4% (or more) compared with existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/ZijiangY1116/PANO.

title: Canonical spin glass behavior and memory effects in van der Waals magnet (Fe0.55Ni0.45)3GaTe2
summary: We demonstrate the canonical spin-glass behavior and non-equilibrium dynamics in a single-crystalline Ni-doped van der Waals magnet (Fe0.55Ni0.45)3GaTe2 with a freezing temperature $T_f \approx 45.5$ K from detailed ac susceptibility and dc magnetization measurements. The temperature-dependent dc magnetization exhibits strong magnetic irreversibility and the ac susceptibility shows that the peak at $T_f$ shifts towards higher temperatures with increase in ac frequency, indicating the presence of a spin glass state. The relative shift of the freezing temperature $δT_f$ per decade of frequency in ac susceptibility is estimated to be 0.0072. Dynamic scaling analysis of the frequency-dependent freezing temperature using the power law reveals the single spin flip relaxation time $τ_0=2\times10^{-13}$ s and critical exponent $zν=8.1$, while the Vogel-Fulcher law yields Vogel-Fulcher temperature $T_0=43$ K and activation energy $E_a/k_B=81$ K with $E_a/k_BT_0=1.88$. The obtained values of these characteristic parameters lie well within the range associated with a canonical spin glass. The detailed non-equilibrium dynamics study, involving the magnetic relaxation and memory effect, further confirms the glassy behavior. The memory effect in zero-field-cooled magnetization establishes that the glassy state arises from the cooperative spin-spin interaction and not from superparamagnetism. The asymmetric response of magnetic relaxation with respect to negative and positive temperature cycle favors the hierarchical model of memory effects over the droplet model.

title: Performance limits and benchmarking of ideal 2D topological insulator field-effect transistors
summary: Topological insulator field-effect transistors (TIFETs) have emerged as a promising alternative to overcome the scaling limits of silicon-based field-effect transistors (Si-based FETs).
